Behind the image

What is calculated, and what is drawn.

A two-dimensional gas of 100 to 600 atoms in a 24 × 14 box is simulated live by molecular dynamics. Atoms are discs (radius 0.16) that repel like stiff springs when they touch, and the walls do the same. Units: mass m = 1, Boltzmann’s constant k = 1, and the average temperature is kT = 1.

xn+1 − 2xn + xn−1 = round(F(xn) Δt² / m)

Exactly reversible

Positions are stored as whole numbers (steps of 10⁻⁷ units), and every force kick is rounded to a whole number before it is applied (the Levesque–Verlet method). Each step then depends only on the current positions, so flipping the velocities retraces every step bit for bit, with no rounding drift. In ordinary floating-point simulations, rounding errors alone would spoil the reversal.

The nudge

With the nudge on, the followed atom is moved sideways by 3 × 10⁻⁷ units (about a millionth of its width) at the moment of reversal. The gas is chaotic: the tiny error grows with each collision until the reversed motion bears no relation to the forward one.

Entropy

The entropy shown is coarse-grained, per atom, in units of k: the box is divided into 8 × 5 counting cells, and S = −Σ p ln p over the share of atoms p in each cell; speeds are counted in rings in each of four vertical strips, which captures hot and cold regions. Both terms are corrected for the finite number of atoms (Miller–Madow). For free expansion it rises by ln 2 ≈ 0.69 per atom, and for the hot and cold halves by ln(Tf/√(ThotTcold)), as thermodynamics predicts; the automated tests check both.

The odds

By Boltzmann’s formula, a state lower in entropy by ΔS per atom is about e−NΔS/k times less likely. For 400 atoms that have spread through the whole box, the chance of all of them being found in the left half again is 2−400 ≈ 1 in 10120.

Touch and keys

Drag to orbit, pinch or scroll to zoom, hover over an atom to read it, click to follow it. Keys: Space pause, 1–3 experiments, B reverse, T 3D/Top, R restart.

Drawn for clarity: colours (blue slow, amber fast; in the heat experiment the floor is tinted by each cell's average energy, smoothed over a few frames), the glow on the followed atom and the height of the speed chart, which rescales to fit. On phones the atoms are drawn 1.7 times larger than their true size. Real gases are 3D and hugely larger (about 1022 atoms in a litre of air), which makes the odds of going backwards unimaginably smaller still. The atoms here are classical; quantum effects are left out.

Further reading: Feynman Lectures, Volume I, chapter 46 · Sean Carroll, From Eternity to Here
